scenes.heading: Deciding when to raise prices and how to communicate it

sents.d: Deciding when to raise prices and how to communicate it
Underpricing out of fear of losing customers usually costs more than the customers you'd actually lose.

A price increase that reflects real cost changes (materials, fuel, time) is easier to justify to customers than one that feels arbitrary — being able to explain the reason briefly, if asked, helps the conversation go smoothly.
Giving existing customers advance notice of a price change, rather than surprising them on their next invoice, preserves trust even when the number itself isn't welcome news.

A price that's too low to sustain the business isn't actually helping customers long-term if it means going out of business — most experienced owners raise prices more often, and more comfortably, than new owners expect to need to.

take: Raise prices when costs rise, with notice and a simple reason.
